list.listitem: Plain X-rays are recommended for acute back pain in patients older than 50 years, those with pain for longer than 1 month, or those with a history of malignancy, corticosteroid use, unexplained weight loss, or previous vertebral compression fracture (VCF). B
Treatment of VCF focuses on pain control with analgesics or calcitonin. B
Patients with severe fractures or neurologic symptoms should be referred for surgical intervention, although data from RCTs on the value of vertebroplasty is conflicting. A

Postmenopausal women with osteoporotic VCF should receive zoledronate, bisphosphonate or teriparatide to prevent additional VCF. Zoledronate 5 mg IV every 18 months to 5 years should be considered in osteopenic women over 65.,A

background.definition: Vertebral compression fractures are defined by isolated fracture of the vertebral anterior column, classically resulting in a wedge deformity.

list.listitem: A total of 15% of women referred for screening bone densitometry in one cohort had evidence of VCF on lateral radiographs.
Trauma.
Osteoporosis (primary or secondary).
Malignancy (metastatic or primary).
Multiple myeloma.
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis are at increased risk as well (pooled RR ~2).

Warfarin use is associated with an increased risk of osteoporotic fracture, including vertebral compression fracture. A study comparing dabigatran with warfarin found a lower risk of osteoporotic fracture among those at high risk for fallse taking dabigatran (NNT = 48).
Long-term use of bisphosphonates in women with osteoporosis is associated with a paradoxically increased risk of fracture.
In osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture (or VCF related to malignancy), the ongoing loss of vertebral trabecular bone results in bone fragility and collapse with minor or no trauma.
Traumatic VCF results from high-energy flexion injuries with disruption of one or both endplates or the anterior cortex.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of fragility fracture in a first-degree relative
Oral corticosteroid use for more than 3 months
Alcohol intake greater than 2 servings per day

list.listitem: Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and VCF should receive a bisphosphonate, zoledronate, or teriparatide to prevent future VCFs. The NNT to prevent a new fracture by giving 35 mg oral risdronate once weekly was 16 over 2 years.A
Routine screening is not recommended. C
Preventive pharmacotherapy is also recommended for men with osteoporosis.,B
Intermittent zoledronic infusions (every 5 years) reduce radiographic fracture risk in women 50 to 60 years with normal bone density or osteopenia. B,
Routine screening for vertebral compression fracture (VCF) is not recommended.

Many elderly patients receive chest X-rays for other reasons and could receive incidental diagnoses. However, one study found that only 60% of VCFs evident on chest X-rays performed on elderly patients in the emergency department were reported, and only 25% of patients received a subsequent diagnosis or treatment of VCF.

Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and VCF should receive a bisphosphonate, zoledronate, or teriparatide to prevent future VCFs. An RCT in 1360 women with severe osteoporisis and previous fracture found that 20 mcg weekly or teriparetide was more effective at preventing new fracture than 35 mg oral risdronate once weekly (5.4% vs 12.0%, p < 0.001, NNT = 16 over 2 years).

A Cochrane review concluded that risedronate was unlikely to be effective for primary prevention of VCF but that it was helpful for secondary prevention in women with a previous VCF (RR 0.8, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.90, absolute risk reduction 2%, NNT = 50).

A study of women 65 and older with osteopenia (T score -1.0 to -2.5 at hip or femoral neck) randomized 2000 to zoledronate 5 mg infusion or a saline infusion every 18 months. At 6 years, the risk of symptomatic vertebral or non-vertebral fracture was lower in the active treatment group (NNT = 64 over 6 years).

A study identified 1054 women 50 to 60 years with normal bone density or osteopenia (T-score 0 to -2.5) and randomized them to receive (1) zoledronate 5 mg IV infusion at baseline plus another zoledronate infusion at 5 years, (2) zoledronate at baseline and placebo infusion at 5 years, or (3) placebo infusions at both times. Radiographic vertebral fractures were observed less often in the 2 groups that received zoledronate (6.3% zol-zol, 6.6% zol-placebo, and 11.1% placebo-placebo; RR 0.58; 95% CI .38 to .87 for both zol arms vs placebo; NNT = 21 to prevent one fracture over 10 years).

A systematic review of 10 RCTs concluded that one would have to give a bisphosphonate to 200 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis for one year to avoid 1 clinical vertebral fracture, assuming a 0.5% annual absolute risk reduction.

For men with low bone mineral density or osteoporosis, a systematic review of 24 studies lasting from 1 to 3 years with 4868 total patients concluded that bisphosphonates reduce the risk of any vertebral fracture (RR 0.37), although the reduction in clinical vertebral fractures was non-significant (RR 0.40; 95% CI 0.11-1.51).

A network meta-analysis of the prevention of VCF in men with osteoporosis found significant benefits with denosumab (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.13-0.68), risedronate (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19-0.77), and zoledronic acid (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.21-0.98) compared to placebo. One agent was not clearly superior to another.
In the absence of high-energy trauma, the history, physical and diagnostic testing for vertebral compression fracture (VCF) should focus on risk factors for malignancy or underlying osteoporosis. C
Plain X-rays are the initial test of choice for diagnosing VCF in patients with acute low back pain and risk factors for osteoporotic VCF or malignancy. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Disruption of middle and/or posterior column on imaging studies
Fever, potential source of infection, typical changes on imaging studies

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: VCFs involve the anterior column only. They are graded on the basis of the loss of vertebral height. Grade 1 (mild): 20% to 25% Grade 2 (moderate): 25% to 40% Grade 3 (severe): >40%

list.listitem: Osteoporotic VCFs are often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on radiographs. The cardinal symptom of osteoporotic or other VCF is localized back pain, especially following trauma in an older person.
Older age, trauma, history of corticosteroid use, or a history of VCF increase the likelihood of osteoporotic VCF.
Plain radiographs are the diagnostic test of choice in patients with suspected osteoporotic VCF or those with only moderate risk factors for malignancy.

MRI or CT is preferred in patients with high risk for malignancy, infection, or trauma-related fracture as these modalities provide additional information about fracture age, vertebral structural integrity, or extension beyond the vertebra. Using MRI as the reference standard, one study of 32 vertebral fractures found that dual energy CT was 90% sensitive and 98% specific.

Laboratory tests are of limited value in evaluating VCF, but may be useful in assessing the likelihood of a malignant etiology. Elevated sedimentation rate (especially greater than 100 mm/hr) and a hematocrit level of less than 30% are strongly associated with malignancy in patients with back pain.
All patients with VCF should undergo bone densitometry to evaluate for osteoporosis.
See algorithm in .
Pain control and the prevention of complications are the cornerstones of management. C
Calcitonin may be used as an alternative to traditional analgesics. B
Two RCTs found that vertebroplasty was no more effective than sham procedures, but a third RCT enrolling patients more acutely (within 6 weeks) found reduced pain at 6 months. B
Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and VCF should receive a bisphosphonate or teriparatide to prevent future VCFs. A
Acute pain control should be obtained with acetaminophen, NSAIDs, tramadol, opioids, or calcitonin.

Medications can reduce the risk for additional VCF in postmenopausal women with prior histories of osteoporotic fracture. Risedronate and etidronate are associated with absolute risk reductions of 5% (number needed to treat [NNT] = 20) and alendronate at 10 mg/day is associated with an absolute risk reduction of 6% (NNT = 16.7).

Teriparatide is a synthetic parathyroid hormone which at doses of 20 and 40 mcg has been associated with absolute risk reductions of 9% and 10%, respectively. In an RCT it was shown to be more effective for secondary prevention of VCF in 1360 women with severe osteoporisis and a previous VCF (NNT = 16 over 2 years to prevent one fracture).
A Cochrane review found moderate quality evidence of no effect of vitamin D and calcium on the prevention of clinical vertebral fractures.

In patients with multiple myeloma, clodronate and pamidronate reduce the risk of fracture (NNT = 10). A Cochrane systematic review of the use of bisphosphonates in patients with multiple myeloma concluded that their use reduces the likelihood of vertebral fracture and pain, but increases the likelihood of osteonecrosis of the jaw (NNH = 1000).

Three well-designed RCTs with appropriate sham comparison found no evidence that vertebroplasty was more effective than a sham in patients enrolled up to one year after their fracture. In these studies, both groups had modest improvement. On the other hand, another RCT recruited 120 patients 60 and older with painful osteoporotic compression fracture within 6 weeks of their fracture, and randomized them to vertebroplasty or sham vertebroplasty. They found a greater likelihood of pain improvement and less analgesic use (NNT = 5-6) at 6 months in those receiving active therapy. The difference suggests that there is potential benefit only with acute therapy (within 6 weeks). However, the most recent study (2018) randomized 180 persons with acute osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture to vertebroplasty or a sham procedure. While both groups reported improvements in pain scores, there was no difference between groups in any outcomes.

A meta-analysis found five studies with 253 patients comparing unilateral with bilateral kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral fracture, and found no difference between the two approaches. However, the overall quality of evidence was limited.

A meta-analysis identified 8 RCTs comparing vertebroplasty with kyphoplasty for osteoporotic compression fractures. While kyphoplasty provided small advantages in terms of less cement leakage and slightly greater vertebral height, all other outcomes were similar.

A subsequent review found 11 RCTs with 1190 patients comparing kyphyplasty with vertebroplasty for vertebral compression fracture and found that kyphoplasty may be superior, with a lower risk of subsequent adjacent vertebral fractures.
For patients with cancer-related vertebral compression fractures, a systematic review concluded that vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty both lead to rapid reduction in pain.

Immobilization of the affected vertebral body alleviates pain but at the risk of deconditioning. An expert consensus statement recommends using orthoses in combination with partial bed rest for short periods (<6 weeks) only. A Korean RCT randomized 60 patients to rigid brace, soft brace, or no brace. At 12 weeks, there was no difference between groups in the Oswestry Disability Index.
Physical therapy and occupational therapy help patients maintain or regain physical conditioning.
Patients with osteoporotic VCF should receive a multidisciplinary fall risk assessment.

A UK study randomized 615 patients to 7 one hour sessions of manual outpatient PT, 7 one hour sessions of exercise outpatient PT, or a single session of PT focused on education about lifestyle and bone health. Minor benefits of the multiple session arms seen at 4 months were no longer seen at one year.
Patients should be monitored for depression.
Traumatic VCF or severe osteoporotic VCF warrant hospitalization to initiate management and to monitor for neurologic instability or adverse reactions to treatment.
Development of neurologic signs or posterior column instability warrants evaluation for surgical intervention.
Ileus develops commonly with lower thoracic or lumbar VCF and the use of opioids. Expectant management is warranted.
Acute pain from osteoporotic VCF is generally self-limited. C
Patients with prior osteoporotic VCF are at a 4-fold or higher risk for future VCF, depending on the number of fractures and the presence of other risk factors. A
Patients with prior osteoporotic VCF—with or without symptoms—are at high risk for recurrent fractures if they are not treated with antiresorptive therapy.
A single VCF increases the risk for another 4 to 5 fractures, while 2 or more VCFs increases the risk 11.8 times. Risk is increased 75-fold for women with low bone mass and multiple VCFs.
Pain from conservatively managed osteoporotic VCF generally resolves over 2 to 12 weeks.
Vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty for osteoporotic VCF may provide more rapid pain relief and more rapid return to function in patients with severe or prolonged pain.
X-rays repeated for worsening symptoms or at 1 month can assess progression, particularly with osteoporotic or malignant VCF.
Prolonged bed rest can cause weakness and should be avoided.
Drinking fluids and eating fiber may help prevent constipation. If you take narcotic medications for pain, talk with your physician about the use of stool softeners or laxatives.

cell.label: Acute low back pain with suspected vertebral compression fracture (VCF)
One or more risk factors for cancer or osteoporotic fracture (previous VCF, osteoporosis, steroid use, older than 50 years, unexplained weight loss, failure to improve after 1 month)?
Treat as musculoskeletal low back pain. Consider imaging if patient does not improve.
